Choice.value: 1 - Clinically consistent and expected given the context (e.g., blood pressure improving after antihypertensive therapy, wound healing progression notes)
2 - Plausible with reasonable clinical explanation (e.g., medication dosage changes over time, symptom improvement with treatment)
3 - Biologically impossible (e.g., patient is both 30 and 73 years old)
4 - Highly implausible physiologically (e.g., lab values swing drastically without explanation)
5 - Possible but doubtful (e.g., stent documented as placed vs not placed)
1 - Trivial inconsistency with no clinical impact (e.g., minor formatting differences)
2 - Minor inconsistency that doesn't affect patient care (e.g., different date formats)
3 - Moderate inconsistency that could cause confusion (e.g., conflicting medication dosages)
4 - Significant inconsistency that could impact clinical decisions (e.g., conflicting diagnoses)
5 - Critical inconsistency that could harm patient safety (e.g., conflicting allergies, incompatible vital signs)
1 - Temporally inappropriate - contradiction easily explained by normal clinical evolution (e.g., 'No fever' on Day 1 vs 'Fever 101°F' on Day 3 during infection treatment)
2 - Poor temporal context - contradiction likely reflects expected clinical progression (e.g., 'Hypertensive crisis' on Day 1 vs 'Blood pressure controlled' on Day 3 with therapy)

3 - Questionable temporal appropriateness - contradiction spans timeframe where some clinical change possible but not expected (e.g., 'No known drug allergies' on Day 1 vs 'Allergic to penicillin' on Day 2 without new exposure)
4 - Good temporal appropriateness - same-day contradictions for conditions that should remain stable (e.g., 'Gallbladder removed in 2015' vs 'Cholelithiasis present' documented on same day)

5 - Optimal temporal appropriateness - contradictions involving immutable historical facts or same-day stable conditions (e.g., 'Previous coronary bypass surgery' vs 'No cardiac surgical history' regardless of timeframe)
